title.narrative: ROAF/SOM/Urban and Territorial Planning for Durable Solutions to Displacement

description.narrative: Somalia has an estimated population of 16.8 million people, of which 3,8 million people or nearly 23 per cent, are internally displaced by conflict, insecurity, drought and floods. Most people have self-settled in over 2,400+ sub-standard IDP sites in urban and peri-urban areas across the country. More than 85% of the sites are informal settlements on private land, and about 74% are in urban areas . People displaced to these sites live in precarious conditions and do not have their basic needs met due to inconsistent service provision or exclusion from accessing humanitarian support. Evictions are commonplace, putting further stress on displaced families and limiting their ability to integrate into social structures. IDP returns to home are extremely limited as many displaced families have lost livelihoods and rely on humanitarian services. Increasing number of displacement waves over the last decades in conjunction with loss of livelihood opportunities, insecurity and non-existing or fragile government structures have dramatically changed the traditional settlement system and clan power dynamics in south central Somalia. This led to long-lasting negative impacts on livelihood, food security, resilience of rural communities and capacities of local and regional authorities; some districts in South West State and Jubaland are still under direct control of terrorist groups and local militias. Furthermore, the increased pressure on already limited resources results in conflicts and friction between the newcomers and hosting communities for access to land, housing, health care, education, basic services, and employment opportunities. This has the potential to put social cohesion and peacebuilding at risk. Apart from a few larger cities, existing coordination and management mechanisms are largely informal, with most sites being managed by informal arrangements between displacement affected communities, local elders and site brokers. Nevertheless, Somalia has made remarkable process under the Durable Solutions Initiative to develop national policies and regulations to tackle protracted displacement. The National Durable Solutions Strategy has been directly linked to the National Development Plan (2020-2024), which also serves as the national Poverty Reduction Strategy document. The political responsibility lies with the national Ministry of Planning, Investment and Economic Development through its Directorate for Poverty Reduction and Durable Solutions. The first steps to managing rapid urbanization have been taken with the elaboration of several spatial plans and district profiles that suggest the future growth and direction of towns in the country. In addition, through support by the UN Joint Programme on Local Governance and Decentralized Service Delivery as well Saameynta – Scaling Up Solutions to Displacement – state initiatives in reforming land governance made progress such as land dispute mechanism, land management information system, but most notably in Puntland and South West State to enact urban land management laws that incorporate a variety of systems and structures for spatial urban development planning with regards to the displacement crises. Nevertheless, there is a long way to operationalize land legislation and invest in capacity building and continued learning from lessons that arise from specific fieldwork and application of various planning tools. However, the continuous influx of migrants, refugees, and displaced persons continues to impose challenges on the urban areas while hindering social, economic, and environmental development. Displacement is far more than a humanitarian challenge for Somalia. In a short period of time, the different cities and towns must assimilate and include large quantities of newcomers into the urban contexts and neighbourhoods. In most cases, the reception of IDPs, returnees and refugees is only possible through the creation and expansion of informal settlements that only perpetuate displacement and inequality by leaving migrants in crowded and precarious conditions. Furthermore, the increased pressure on already limited resources results in conflicts and friction between the newcomers and hosting communities for access to land, housing, health care, education, basic services, and employment opportunities. This has the potential to put social cohesion and peacebuilding at risk. It furthermore leads to new view on the interlinkages between space and “people on the move” as actors involved in Durable Solutions Programming increasingly look into conditions that trigger rural-urban movements, but also into the conditions that would strengthen urban-rural linkages hence that displacement waves over the last decades have dramatically changed the traditional settlement system in south central Somalia with wide ranging negative impact on livelihood, food security, resilience of rural communities and local governance structures.
